title: In Search of Memory: The Emergence of a New Science of Mind
author: Eric R. Kandel
note: Selected for the praised-book intake: specialist reviews by Yadin Dudai, Solomon Snyder and Francis Mechner, plus a strong reader aggregate. This is explanatory scientific autobiography, not neuroscience training. Personal persecution and Vienna frame the scientific life but do not predominate; T11=0. Experimental memory research is central, so T12=0. Scientific-biography exception also applies to V3. Terminological objections to reductionism have substantive defenses and do not establish V9 at high confidence. Later speculative extensions must be separated from the core experimental findings.
notes: First-hand experimental account with specialist corroboration; autobiographical selection and speculative extensions prevent full attainment.
Connects molecular processes, neural circuits, behavior and research organization; limited production or economic integration.
Strong lessons in choosing tractable model systems and research questions; transfer beyond experimental science is less direct.
Links experimental intervention to mechanisms of short- and long-term memory, rather than relying only on correlation.

D=8/10, moderate confidence from the detailed Mechner review, Dudai and Snyder reviews, and contents. Distinct experiments and changes in research strategy add learning; autobiographical passages vary in direct scientific yield. No full-text audit claimed.
Research history and experimental reasoning remain useful; the book is not a current survey of all neuroscience.
Good fit for scientific method and organization, less direct for computing or industrial scaling.
Nobel-winning investigator, assessed favorably by several named specialists.
Personal chronology and experimental development form a readable cumulative account.
Specialist reviewers support clear and careful exposition; technical metaphors require context.

title: Genius Makers: The Mavericks Who Brought AI to Google, Facebook, and the World
author: Cade Metz
note: Selected on named expert praise from Kai-Fu Lee and Oren Etzioni (publisher-reproduced endorsements), professional reviews and a strong reader aggregate. These endorsements are not independent peer review. Kamdar's low personal rating is contrary evidence and is retained rather than treated as praise. The book explains the people, institutions and commercial rise of deep learning; it is not a technical curriculum. International research and industry are central; T11=T12=0. Its historical value does not require its forward-looking expectations to prove correct. No serious veto established, but it must not be read as a current technical survey.
notes: Extensive interview reporting supports the historical account; access-driven narrative and predictions remain less secure than documented events.
Connects university research, computing resources, corporate acquisition, finance and international competition.
Useful for understanding talent concentration, research incentives and commercialization; fewer explicit decision models.
Institutional causes are clearer than the technical mechanisms of neural-network performance.

D=7/10, moderate confidence from professional reviews, source reading report and publisher sample description. Research milestones and acquisitions add distinct cases; a large cast and personality detail reduce learning yield for a technically trained reader.
The institutional history retains value, while contemporary capabilities and forecasts date quickly.
Direct fit for computing, scientific organization and technology adoption.
Experienced technology reporter with substantial access and named expert endorsement; not himself an AI research authority.
Accessible character-driven account, with some fragmentation from the large cast.
Readable explanations, occasionally relying on broad technology labels.
